canonical_answers.title: Fuel-Water Emulsification (FWE) to Reduce Diesel Engine NOx Emissions
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Fuel-Water Emulsification system, with a sketch (12)**

**[Sketch]** Fuel-Water Emulsification system — D.O. and HFO tanks, supply pumps, emergency air-driven pump, homogenizer with H₂O feed, circulating pump, pre-heater, safety tank, venting box, full-flow filter, water sensor, main engine, fuel oil drain tank.

The FWE system reduces NOx emissions by introducing controlled amounts of water into the fuel before combustion. Fuel (D.O. or HFO) is pumped from storage tanks by supply pumps, with an emergency air-driven pump ensuring supply during pump failure. The fuel passes through a homogenizer, where water is added and mixed to form a stable, uniform emulsion, then fed to the circulating pump for consistent flow and pressure. Before entering the engine, the emulsified fuel is preheated to the desired viscosity and passes through a full-flow filter and a water sensor monitoring water content. Excess fuel returns to the system, with separated water drained to the fuel oil drain tank; a venting box and safety tank manage pressure fluctuations.

The NOx-reduction mechanism is the micro-explosion effect: as fuel droplets reach the high-temperature combustion chamber, the water inside rapidly vaporises, causing the droplets to break into finer particles (improving air-fuel mixing) while absorbing latent heat and lowering local combustion temperature. Since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this reduces NOx significantly; the water also promotes slower, more uniform combustion, preventing the localised hot spots that are primary NOx sources, and reduces particulate-forming fuel-rich zones. Overall, FWE can reduce NOx emissions by 30–50%.

**(b) Disadvantages of this method (4)**

Engine efficiency may be affected, as water addition reduces the fuel's energy content, causing a slight rise in fuel consumption for the same power output. Corrosion and wear risk on fuel system components is higher due to water presence, accelerating oxidation and erosion. Maintaining a stable emulsion requires precise monitoring and control — poorly mixed emulsions cause incomplete combustion, increased carbon deposits, and potential engine damage. The system also requires additional equipment and modifications, raising installation and maintenance costs.

canonical_answers.title: SOx Exhaust Gas Cleaning — Monitored Parameters & Sea-Pollution Prevention
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) System parameters monitored, monitoring device location, data storage & availability to regulators (10)**

Key parameters: the SO₂/CO₂ ratio (gas analysers in the exhaust duct, verifying SOx stays within permissible limits); pH level of discharge water (measured at the washwater discharge outlet, to prevent acidic effluent harming marine life); turbidity (suspended particles in discharge water, for opacity compliance); polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) concentration (sensors in the washwater discharge line, to prevent oil pollution from scrubber effluent); temperature (at the washwater discharge point, to prevent thermal pollution); washwater flow rate (flow meters, ensuring adequate water for SOx removal); pressure drop across the scrubber (differential pressure sensors, detecting blockages/inefficiency); and, for open-loop systems, alkalinity at the scrubber inlet (ensuring effective SOx absorption and pH control).

Data is stored in the ship's onboard EGCS data recording system, typically integrated with the ship's automation system, continuously logged and accessible via digital logs, printouts or electronic submissions. Flag states, port state control and classification societies require this data available for inspection; modern installations may also feature remote monitoring for real-time compliance tracking.

**(b) How SOx cleaning systems can pollute sea water, and prevention (6)**

*Pollution causes*: acidification (open-loop scrubbers discharge acidic washwater, lowering sea pH and affecting ecosystems); heavy-metal contamination (vanadium, nickel, lead in discharge); oil/PAH pollution (hydrocarbons mixing into washwater); increased turbidity (particulate matter reducing light penetration for aquatic life); thermal pollution (discharge significantly warmer than ambient seawater).

*Prevention*: pH neutralisation (alkaline dosing, e.g. sodium hydroxide, to keep discharge pH above regulatory limits); filtration and treatment (washwater filtration and sludge removal to capture metals/particles); PAH monitoring (sensors ensuring hydrocarbon levels stay within limits); closed-loop or hybrid systems (recycling washwater instead of direct discharge, or switching modes); and compliance with MARPOL Annex VI via regular inspection and documentation of washwater quality.

canonical_answers.title: SCR Chemical Supply System — Safety/Pollution Avoidance & NOx Reduction Chemistry
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Diesel engine NOx reduction system chemical supply — sketch, safety & pollution avoidance (12)**

**[Sketch]** SCR chemical supply system — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia sensing lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

SCR reduces NOx via controlled injection of ammonia (or urea solution) into the exhaust, reacting with NOx over a catalyst to form harmless N₂ and H₂O, meeting IMO Tier III. The reagent is stored in a dedicated tank and pumped through double-skinned pipe (safety); an evaporator and dosing pump prepare the correct quantity for engine load/exhaust conditions. A static mixer blends ammonia into the exhaust stream, with air supplied below the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) to eliminate combustion risk; the mixed gas passes through a receiver before the SCR reactor. A bypass valve allows exhaust to skip the SCR unit if needed, for continuous engine operation during a system fault.

Safety/pollution-avoidance features: double-skinned piping (prevents ammonia leaks); flow-rate, temperature, NOx and ammonia-slip sensors (performance/compliance monitoring); a safety valve (releases excess pressure); and dynamic injection-rate adjustment (limits ammonia slip — unreacted ammonia that would otherwise pollute the atmosphere). Proper temperature control and flow regulation optimise catalyst efficiency for effective NOx reduction under MARPOL Annex VI.

**(b) Chemical reactions involved (4)**

Urea thermally decomposes to ammonia and CO₂:

CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂

Ammonia then reacts with NOx over a vanadium/titanium/zeolite-based catalyst. For NO:

4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O

For NO₂:

6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O

Where the exhaust contains a mix of NO and NO₂, the optimal 1:1 reaction is:

NO + NO₂ + 2NH₃ → 2N₂ + 3H₂O

The system minimises ammonia slip — excess unreacted ammonia released to atmosphere as secondary pollution — through continuous monitoring of NOx levels, temperature and injection rate.

canonical_answers.title: Why Efficient Engines Produce More NOx + SCR Unit Description + Monitoring Exhaust Flows
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why highly efficient diesel engines tend to produce more NOx (4)**

Higher efficiency comes from higher combustion temperatures and pressure ratios, and NOx formation is directly temperature-dependent — nitrogen and oxygen react at high temperature to form NO/NO₂. Advanced fuel injection and turbocharging improve air-fuel mixing, raising peak combustion temperature; efficient engines also run leaner (excess oxygen), further promoting NOx formation. Environmental regulation therefore requires after-treatment technologies such as SCR to offset this trade-off.

**(b) SCR unit for a marine propulsion diesel engine (8)**

**[Sketch]** Selective Catalytic Reduction unit — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

(As described in the SCR chemical-supply canonical: ammonia/urea stored and dosed via evaporator and pump, mixed into the exhaust via a static mixer with sub-LEL air, reacted over the catalyst, with a bypass valve for system faults.) Efficiency depends on accurate reagent dosing and maintaining the SCR's optimal temperature range (typically 250–450°C) for effective NOx conversion, ensuring IMO Tier III compliance under MARPOL Annex VI.

**(c) Why exhaust gas flow monitoring in/out of the SCR is required, and how readings control chemical dosing (4)**

Flow rate, temperature and NOx concentration are measured at both SCR inlet and outlet. These readings set the precise reagent dose: too little reagent leaves NOx reduction incomplete (excess emissions); too much causes ammonia slip (unreacted ammonia released to atmosphere, a pollution and compliance risk). The SCR control unit adjusts injection rate in real time based on these readings and changing engine load/fuel type, keeping the system within IMO Tier III limits while minimising ammonia-related pollution.

canonical_answers.title: External NOx Reduction System (SCR) — Chemistry, Urea vs Ammonia, Exhaust-Gas-Quality Monitoring
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) External NOx reduction system (SCR), with chemistry (8)**

**[Sketch]** External NOx reduction system (SCR) — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

Ammonia solution, stored in a dedicated tank and pumped via double-skinned pipe, is prepared by an evaporator and dosing pump and injected via a static mixer into the exhaust stream (with sub-LEL air for safety), before passing through a receiver into the SCR reactor. A bypass valve allows exhaust to skip the unit if needed. Reaction chemistry: 4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O and 6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O.

**(b) Why urea is used instead of ammonia (4)**

Ammonia is toxic and hazardous, requiring specialised pressurised or refrigerated storage. Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) is a stable, non-toxic solid or aqueous solution that is easily stored and transported; injected into the exhaust, it thermally decomposes to release ammonia in a controlled way: CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂ — reducing ammonia-slip and environmental-hazard risk versus direct ammonia handling.

**(c) Why exhaust gas quality is monitored before and after the SCR unit, and how this affects operation (4)**

Sensors measure NOx concentration, temperature and ammonia level. Pre-SCR monitoring determines the correct reagent dose (too little → incomplete NOx reduction; too much → ammonia slip and pollution). Post-SCR monitoring confirms compliance with IMO Tier III and that no excess ammonia is released. This closed-loop monitoring optimises reagent consumption, maintains catalytic efficiency, and prevents damage from unreacted-ammonia deposits.

canonical_answers.title: SCR + Fuel Sulphur Content Effects & Turbocharger Interaction — Dual-Path System
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Influence of fuel sulphur content on SCR operation, with a graph (4)**

**[Graph]** Temperature upstream of SCR (250–370°C) vs sulphur content (0–4.0%).

High-sulphur fuel combustion produces SO₂ and some SO₃, which react with the ammonia injected for NOx reduction, forming ammonium bisulphate (NH₄HSO₄) and ammonium sulphate ((NH₄)₂SO₄):

SO₃ + NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄HSO₄
SO₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O → (NH₄)₂SO₄

These sulphate deposits condense at relatively high temperature (250–300°C), blocking and fouling the SCR catalyst and reducing effectiveness over time, increasing cleaning/maintenance costs. Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) formation from SO₃ and water condensation can also corrode the turbocharger, economiser and SCR reactor housing, especially if exhaust temperature drops too low at low engine load. Mitigations: exhaust gas heating to keep temperature above 300–350°C (preventing bisulphate deposition), and/or an SOx scrubber upstream of the SCR to cut sulphur content before it reaches the catalyst.

**(b) How turbocharger operation can detrimentally affect the SCR unit when burning high-sulphur fuel (4)**

High-sulphur fuel raises SOx, which can react with SCR ammonia injection to form ammonium bisulphate; if exhaust temperature is low, this condenses on the turbocharger turbine blades, causing corrosion/fouling that reduces turbocharger efficiency and can lead to surging or eventual failure. Turbochargers also reduce exhaust gas temperature (especially at lower loads), which can fall below the SCR's optimal range (250–450°C), further increasing bisulphate deposition risk on both SCR catalyst and turbocharger components. Mitigations include engine tuning adjustments, exhaust gas bypass systems, or waste-heat-recovery modifications to keep exhaust temperature adequate for SCR operation while protecting the turbocharger.

**(c) A system maintaining good turbocharger performance and good NOx reduction when burning high-sulphur fuel, meeting the conflicting conditions (8)**

**[Sketch]** Dual-path SCR/turbocharger arrangement — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, sensing lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

A dual-path exhaust arrangement combines: an **SCR bypass system** (allows exhaust to partially/fully bypass the SCR at low load, when temperatures are too low to prevent bisulphate formation); an **exhaust gas heater/heat-retention system** (waste-heat recovery or exhaust gas burner raising temperature before the SCR reactor, reducing sulphate-deposition risk); a **turbocharger protection mechanism** (dedicated heat exchanger or air bypass regulating turbocharger-inlet gas temperature, preventing condensation of corrosive sulphur compounds on turbine blades); an **SOx scrubber upstream of the SCR** (removing most sulphur oxides before the SCR reactor); and an **intelligent ammonia-injection control system** (adjusting dosing based on real-time exhaust temperature and sulphur content, optimising NOx reduction while avoiding excess ammonia slip).

canonical_answers.title: Diesel Engine NOx Emissions & Control — EGR/DWI CO2 Trade-Off + Selective Catalytic Reduction System
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) How EGR and Direct Water Injection reduce NOx but raise specific CO2 emissions (6)**

In EGR, a portion of exhaust gas is recirculated into the intake air, reducing available oxygen and peak combustion temperature; since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this suppresses thermal NOx. However, reduced oxygen causes less complete combustion, lowering engine efficiency and raising specific fuel consumption (SFC) — and since CO₂ is directly tied to fuel burned, specific CO₂ emissions rise per unit power.

Direct Water Injection similarly injects water into the combustion chamber/intake to absorb heat and lower peak temperature, suppressing NOx — but also reduces combustion completeness/thermal efficiency, requiring more fuel for the same power output and again raising CO₂ per kWh.

Both methods trade NOx reduction for efficiency, requiring careful optimisation to balance emissions control against fuel economy.

**(b) Selective Catalytic Reduction system, with monitoring/control systems required**

**[Sketch]** Selective Catalytic Reduction system — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

SCR chemically converts NOx to N₂ and H₂O using ammonia as the reducing agent, meeting IMO Tier III. Key components: ammonia tank, pump/evaporator, static mixer (thorough blending before the reactor), receiver, and SCR reactor, with a bypass for low-load/fault conditions.

Monitoring/control required: NOx sensors at SCR inlet and outlet (verify emissions stay within regulatory limits); ammonia-slip sensors (detect unreacted ammonia before atmospheric release); exhaust temperature monitoring (the catalyst has an effective operating range — too low reduces conversion efficiency, too high risks catalyst damage); and a controller that adjusts ammonia injection rate in real time against NOx level and engine load, backed by pressure-relief/safety valves for safe ammonia handling. All data is logged for real-time diagnostics and compliance reporting (verifiable at port inspections under MARPOL Annex VI).

canonical_answers.title: Hybrid SOx Scrubber Systems — Open/Closed Loop Fluids, When Used, Closed-Loop Effectiveness & Sea-Pollution Avoidance
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Fluids used in open and closed loops, and how controlled to meet scrubbing demand (6)**

In open-loop mode, seawater is the scrubbing medium — its natural alkalinity neutralises SOx; seawater is drawn in, used for scrubbing, then discharged overboard once meeting discharge limits. In closed-loop mode, freshwater dosed with an alkaline additive (usually sodium hydroxide, NaOH) is continuously recirculated with minimal discharge. Scrubbing efficiency is controlled by adjusting fluid flow rate, NaOH dosing and water pH against engine load — higher loads producing more SOx require higher flow/dosing, lower loads less.

**(b) When Open Loop vs Closed Loop scrubbing is used (2)**

Open-loop scrubbing is used in open seas, where seawater alkalinity is high and regulations permit discharge of treated washwater. Closed-loop scrubbing is used in Emission Control Areas (ECAs) and ports, where discharge regulations are strict and open-loop discharge is restricted.

**(c) Maintaining closed-loop neutralising effectiveness over long periods, and avoiding sea pollution (8)**

As SOx reacts with NaOH, the fluid's alkalinity falls over time, so additional NaOH is dosed to maintain effective scrubbing, with pH and NaOH concentration continuously monitored and adjusted. To prevent pollution, a water treatment unit removes sludge and particulate matter before any treated washwater is discharged; sludge (containing sulphates and impurities) is collected in holding tanks for shore disposal, ensuring no acidic or contaminated discharge reaches the sea, per IMO regulations.

canonical_answers.title: Open Loop / Closed Loop SOx Scrubber (Describe Either) + Monitoring for IMO Compliance
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Describe EITHER an Open Loop OR a Closed Loop SOx scrubber system (10)**

**[Sketch]** Open Loop — scrubber exhaust, exhaust gas in, seawater in, washwater treatment, separated residue, scrubber overboard.

An Open Loop system uses seawater's natural alkalinity to neutralise SOx: exhaust gas is directed into a scrubber tower where sprayed seawater dissolves SO₂ (forming sulfurous acid, further oxidising to sulphuric acid), which the seawater's alkalinity neutralises into calcium sulphate and other harmless salts. Treated exhaust is released to atmosphere; washwater passes through a treatment unit separating solids/sludge for port disposal, with remaining treated water discharged overboard under MARPOL Annex VI limits (pH, turbidity, PAH). Advantages: no chemical additives, lower complexity/cost. Limitations: reduced efficiency in low-alkalinity waters, and many ports/ECAs restrict or ban open-loop discharge.

**[Sketch]** Closed Loop — exhaust gas, scrubber, NaOH unit, fresh water, process tank, water treatment, sludge tank, holding tank, cooler, pumps.

Alternatively, a Closed Loop system recirculates fresh washwater dosed with NaOH, reacting with SO₂ to form dissolved sodium sulphate; washwater passes to a process tank for filtration/treatment, is recirculated, with sludge sent to a holding tank for port disposal (any overboard discharge must still meet MARPOL Annex VI). A cooling system maintains scrubber temperature. Advantages: works in low-alkalinity/ECA waters where open-loop is restricted, minimal direct discharge. Trade-offs: NaOH replenishment, sludge-related maintenance, higher operating cost.

**(b) Systems to monitor to ensure IMO compliance (6)**

Exhaust gas emissions (continuous emission monitoring systems measuring SO₂/CO₂ ratio against the 0.50% global or 0.10% ECA sulphur cap); washwater quality (pH ≥6.5 at the overboard discharge point, turbidity, PAH concentration); scrubber flow rate (accurate pumping/recirculation control for effective SOx removal); in closed-loop systems, NaOH concentration (proper neutralisation); and sludge/residue management (logged collection and disposal to port reception facilities). All monitoring data is logged and made available to port state control for compliance verification.

canonical_answers.title: Open Loop System (In Open Waters) + Closed Loop System (Stating When Used) — Both Described
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Open loop system for reducing SOx, explaining operation whilst the vessel is in open waters (6)**

Seawater is pumped into the scrubber and sprayed over the exhaust gas; its natural alkalinity in open ocean waters neutralises the dissolved SO₂/sulphuric acid into harmless salts, with treated washwater discharged overboard — viable specifically because open-water seawater alkalinity is high enough for effective, compliant neutralisation without chemical additives.

**(b) Closed loop scrubber system for removing SOx, and stating when it would be used (10)**

A closed-loop system recirculates freshwater dosed with an alkaline additive (NaOH) to neutralise SO₂ into dissolved sodium sulphate, with the washwater treated and recirculated rather than continuously discharged; sludge is collected for port disposal, and a cooling system keeps the scrubber within operating temperature limits. It is used specifically in areas where open-loop discharge is restricted or seawater alkalinity is too low for effective open-loop scrubbing — Emission Control Areas, ports, and freshwater/low-salinity waters — since it does not depend on ambient seawater chemistry.

canonical_answers.title: NOx Formation Mechanism + ONE External Reduction Method (Efficiency Trade-Off)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) How NOx is formed, and why the aim of high engine efficiency increases the problem (6)**

NOx forms from the high-temperature combustion process: intake air (~78% N₂, 21% O₂) reacts above ~1,300°C via the Zeldovich mechanism, which is strongly temperature-dependent. Higher efficiency is typically achieved by raising combustion temperature and pressure (better fuel atomisation, higher thermal efficiency) — but this directly intensifies NOx formation, and efficient engines' leaner air-fuel mixtures (excess oxygen) further promote it. So while higher efficiency cuts fuel consumption and CO₂, it worsens NOx, creating an inherent efficiency/NOx trade-off.

**(b) ONE external means of reducing NOx to meet current regulations (10)**

Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR): ammonia or a urea-based solution is injected into the exhaust upstream of a catalytic reactor. Urea decomposes to ammonia at high temperature; the ammonia then reacts with NOx over the catalyst (4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O; 6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O), converting it to harmless nitrogen and water and meeting IMO Tier III limits. SCR operates optimally within a specific exhaust temperature range (roughly 270–450°C), making temperature monitoring essential; NOx sensors, ammonia-slip monitors and exhaust-temperature control regulate injection and prevent excess ammonia escaping. SCR is widely used in marine applications, capable of NOx reductions up to ~90%, but requires careful maintenance (urea consumption monitoring, preventing injection-system crystallisation, catalyst condition) to remain effective.

canonical_answers.title: Diesel Engine Exhaust Emissions — Causes & Effects of CO, CO2, Hydrocarbons & Particulate Matter
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Carbon Monoxide (CO) (4)**

Produced by incomplete combustion when insufficient oxygen is available (poor air-fuel mixing, low excess-air ratio, faulty injectors). Highly toxic — reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, causing CO poisoning; in the atmosphere it contributes to ground-level ozone formation, harming air quality.

**(b) Carbon Dioxide (CO2) (4)**

A natural product of complete combustion (carbon in fuel fully reacting with oxygen). CO₂ output is directly proportional to fuel consumption. Its major effect is contribution to global warming/climate change as a greenhouse gas trapping atmospheric heat.

**(c) Hydrocarbons (HC) (4)**

Unburned hydrocarbons result from incomplete combustion (poor fuel atomisation, low combustion temperature, malfunctioning injectors). They react with NOx in sunlight to form photochemical smog, harmful to health and the environment; some hydrocarbons are also carcinogenic.

**(d) Particulate Matter (PM) (4)**

Soot — fine carbon particles, metal oxides and unburned hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion, associated with poor fuel quality, excessive load, or inefficient combustion. Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs, causing respiratory disease (asthma, lung cancer), and contribute to atmospheric haze reducing visibility.

canonical_answers.title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System — Sketch, Operating & Thermal Efficiency Problems
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) EGR system, with a sketch, and how it reduces NOx (12)**

**[Sketch]** Exhaust Gas Recirculation system — turbocharger, exhaust, intake, scrubber with sea-water inlet/outlet, gas cooler for EGR with S.W. inlet/outlet, EGR blower, cylinder, air cooler.

Exhaust gas leaves the cylinder and passes through the turbocharger; part is diverted through a control valve into the EGR system, entering a scrubber where seawater removes SOx and particulate matter. The scrubbed gas passes through a gas cooler (seawater-cooled) before the EGR blower, which recirculates the cleaned, cooled gas into the engine's air intake, through the air cooler, and into the cylinder for combustion. By diluting intake air with cooled exhaust gas, the system lowers oxygen concentration and peak combustion temperature — since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this significantly suppresses thermal NOx formation, helping meet IMO Tier III limits.

**(b) Operating and thermal-efficiency problems with EGR (4)**

- **Increased soot/carbon deposits**: recirculated exhaust raises unburned hydrocarbon/particulate levels in the combustion chamber, fouling the turbocharger and intake valves, raising maintenance costs and reducing performance.
- **Reduced combustion efficiency**: lower intake oxygen reduces combustion efficiency, raising fuel consumption for the same power output — indirectly increasing CO₂ emissions.
- **Higher exhaust/thermal stress**: recirculating exhaust increases heat retention, raising thermal stress on components and potentially shortening part life/reducing cooling-system efficiency.
- **Potential power loss**: less available oxygen can reduce power output, particularly at high load, requiring fuel-injection strategy adjustments that can further hurt fuel economy.

canonical_answers.title: Dual-Fuel Four-Stroke Combustion Process (Pilot Injection) + Exhaust Gas Recirculation Explained
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Gas combustion process in a dual-fuel medium-speed main engine with pilot injection (10)**

**[Sketch]** Dual-fuel gas combustion process — intake of air and gas / compression of air and gas / ignition by pilot diesel fuel.

A dual-fuel four-stroke engine uses both gaseous fuel (e.g. natural gas) and a small pilot quantity of liquid diesel to guarantee reliable ignition, across the standard intake/compression/power/exhaust strokes. During intake, the intake valve opens first for scavenge air; once air flow is positive, the gas admission valve opens to introduce gaseous fuel, ensuring proper mixing and preventing manifold gas accumulation. Near the end of induction, the gas valve closes first, then the intake valve, for precise fuel control.

During compression (both valves closed), the piston compresses the air-fuel mixture; since the gaseous fuel doesn't auto-ignite at this temperature, a small pilot diesel injection just before TDC ignites under high pressure/temperature, and this flame front then ignites the gas-air mixture — the power stroke. During exhaust, the exhaust valve opens and burnt gases are expelled before the cycle repeats.

The fuel control system continuously balances gas and pilot-fuel quantity for optimal power/emissions, and can automatically switch to diesel-only mode if gas supply is interrupted; electronic control optimises delivery for load and operating conditions.

**(b) What Exhaust Gas Recirculation means, and how it reduces air pollution (6)**

EGR recirculates a controlled portion of exhaust gas back into the intake, diverted from the exhaust manifold and mixed with fresh air (typically cooled via an EGR cooler) before combustion. This dilutes intake oxygen and lowers peak combustion temperature — since NOx formation rises sharply with temperature, the cooler, slower burn significantly reduces NOx output, helping the engine meet emission regulations.
